Keep the covered tray warm (around 74 °F) and dark for a week or two while the seeds slowly sprout, then uncover into bright light (about 68 to 72 °F) for roughly 18 hours a day until the leaves green up. Most are ready in about 3 to 4 weeks.
seasoned: The cycle is sow, blackout, light, harvest, but cilantro is one of the slowest microgreens. Germinate at about 74 °F under a weighted cover in the dark; germination is slow and uneven and the blackout runs long (about 7 to 14 days). Uncover into 18 hours of light at about 68 to 72 °F to green up, then cut at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage. Most trays finish in about 21 to 28 days.

beginner: To always have cilantro microgreens ready, start a new tray every week or two instead of one big batch. Because they grow indoors, you can keep this going all year, just spaced out since cilantro is slow.
seasoned: For a steady supply, stagger sowings, but space them wider than fast microgreens: start a fresh cilantro tray about every 1 to 2 weeks rather than one big tray at once. Indoors there is no season, so the cadence is limited by tray count and cilantro's long 3 to 4 week cycle.

beginner: Cilantro microgreens are baby cilantro plants that you harvest young, once the first little leaves are open, for a strong, fresh cilantro flavor. If you cook with cilantro, this is the microgreen for you, but be warned: cilantro is one of the slowest microgreens to grow. It sprouts slowly and unevenly and usually takes about 3 to 4 weeks, much longer than quick types like radish or broccoli. The round cilantro seed is actually a little dry fruit holding two seeds; some growers crack it into halves or soak it to help it sprout more evenly. You grow it indoors all year on a shallow tray, with no outdoor season or weather to worry about, so it grows the same way no matter where you live, it just takes patience.
seasoned: Cilantro microgreens are the young seedlings of Coriandrum sativum (cilantro, a member of the carrot and parsley family, Apiaceae), grown indoors and cut at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage for true, concentrated cilantro flavor. They are the crop for cooks who love cilantro, but they are also one of the slowest and most demanding microgreens: germination is slow and uneven, the blackout runs long, and a typical tray takes about 21 to 28 days, far longer than the 1 to 2 weeks of fast brassicas. The seed is really a small dry fruit that holds two seeds, sown whole or split (cracked) into halves; splitting or a soak can even out the ragged germination. Because there is no frost, season, or hardiness zone involved, the same tray grows identically on a windowsill anywhere, it just asks for patience.

beginner: Your cilantro microgreens are ready when the first little seed-leaves are open and the first true leaf is just showing, usually about 3 to 4 weeks after sowing. Snip them just above the soil with clean scissors and eat them fresh. They do not grow back, so you start a new tray each time.
seasoned: Cut at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage, typically 21 to 28 days from sowing, one of the longest waits among microgreens. Snip just above the medium with clean scissors; the stand will not regrow, so the tray is a single cut.
